title: Matter, Chemical Trends and Chemical Bonding
seo_title: Grade 11 Chemistry (SCH3U): Matter, Chemical Trends and Chemical Bonding Worksheets (Ontario)
standard_text: Atomic structure and isotopes; the periodic table and periodic trends (atomic radius, ionization energy, electron affinity, electronegativity); ionic and covalent bonding; Lewis structures; polar bonds and intermolecular forces. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Chemistry, Grade 11, University Preparation (SCH3U), Strand B: Matter, Chemical Trends, and Chemical Bonding)
meta_desc: Free Grade 11 Chemistry (SCH3U) worksheets on matter, periodic trends and bonding: isotopes, atomic radius, ionization energy, electronegativity, ionic and covalent bonds, polarity and intermolecular forces. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Periodic trends come from nuclear charge and the number of electron shells.
key_sub: Bond type depends on the electronegativity difference.
body_html:
How to think about it

Across a period, the nuclear charge rises while the number of shells stays the same, so atoms get smaller and ionization energy and electronegativity increase. Down a group, more shells are added, so atoms get larger and hold their outer electrons less tightly.

A large electronegativity difference (more than about 1.7) gives an ionic bond; a smaller difference gives a polar covalent bond, and no difference a non-polar covalent bond. Polar molecules attract each other with dipole–dipole forces; molecules with H bonded to N, O or F form hydrogen bonds, which raise boiling points.

Example

Which has the larger atomic radius, Na or Cl?

Same period; Cl has more protons pulling the electrons in.

Answer: Na

Example

Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37: how are they different?

Same protons (17)

Different neutrons

Answer: chlorine-37 has two more neutrons

Common mistakes

  • Thinking atoms get bigger across a period because they gain electrons.
  • Calling every bond with a metal and a non-metal covalent.
  • Confusing intramolecular bonds (inside molecules) with intermolecular forces (between molecules).

faq.a: How strongly an atom attracts the shared electrons in a bond. Fluorine has the highest value.

faq.q: Why does water have a high boiling point for its size?
faq.a: Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other, which take extra energy to break.

items.q: How many more neutrons does <sup>58</sup>Fe have than <sup>56</sup>Fe?
How many neutrons are in an atom of fluorine-21?
items.e: Neutrons = mass number − atomic number = 21 − 9 = 12.

items.q: How many neutrons are in <sup>4</sup><sub>2</sub>He?
Sofia finds that element X has two isotopes: 90% has mass 31 u and 10% has mass 33 u. What is the relative atomic mass?
Emma finds that element X has two isotopes: 80% has mass 53 u and 20% has mass 55 u. What is the relative atomic mass?
A neutral atom of <sup>206</sup><sub>82</sub>Pb has how many particles (protons, neutrons and electrons) in total?
items.e: 206 nucleons + 82 electrons = 288.

items.q: How many neutrons are in the nucleus <sup>63</sup><sub>29</sub>Cu?
items.e: Neutrons = nucleon number − proton number = 63 − 29 = 34.

items.q: Benjamin finds that element X has two isotopes: 85% has mass 69 u and 15% has mass 71 u. What is the relative atomic mass?
A neutral atom of selenium has a mass number of 80. How many electrons does it have?
items.e: In a neutral atom, electrons = protons = 34.

items.q: Gold-197 and gold-198 are isotopes. What do they have the same number of?
items.e: Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons.

items.q: How many protons are in an atom of selenium-80?
items.e: The atomic number (34) is the number of protons.

items.q: Silver-107 and silver-108 are isotopes. What do they have the same number of?
items.e: Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons.

items.q: A neutral atom of copper has a mass number of 64. How many electrons does it have?
items.e: In a neutral atom, electrons = protons = 29.

items.q: How many protons are in an atom of copper-65?
items.e: The atomic number (29) is the number of protons.

items.q: How many more neutrons does <sup>128</sup>I have than <sup>127</sup>I?
Maya finds that element X has two isotopes: 25% has mass 48 u and 75% has mass 50 u. What is the relative atomic mass?
Calculate the specific charge of the nucleus <sup>210</sup><sub>84</sub>Po. Take the mass of a nucleon as 1.67 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg.
items.e: Specific charge = charge ÷ mass = (84 × 1.60 × 10−19) ÷ (210 × 1.67 × 10−27) = 3.83 × 107 C/kg.

items.q: Calculate the specific charge of the nucleus <sup>238</sup><sub>92</sub>U. Take the mass of a nucleon as 1.67 × 10<sup>−27</sup> kg.
items.e: Specific charge = charge ÷ mass = (92 × 1.60 × 10−19) ÷ (238 × 1.67 × 10−27) = 3.70 × 107 C/kg.

items.q: Which pair are isotopes of the same element?
items.e: Same atomic number, different mass numbers.

items.q: A neutral atom of <sup>222</sup><sub>86</sub>Rn has how many particles (protons, neutrons and electrons) in total?
items.e: 222 nucleons + 86 electrons = 308.

items.q: Which element has chemical properties most like selenium (Se)?
items.e: Same group = same number of valence electrons.

items.q: Which is the largest ion: Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ or F⁻?
items.e: These are isoelectronic; the one with the fewest protons is largest.

items.q: In which group of the periodic table is Ir (Z = 77)?
items.e: Ir is in group 9 (the d-block).

items.q: In which group of the periodic table is Po (Z = 84)?
items.e: Po is in group 16 (the p-block).

items.q: Which element has chemical properties most like argon (Ar)?
items.e: Same group = same number of valence electrons.

items.q: Which family does strontium (Sr) belong to?
items.e: Group 2 is the alkaline earth metals.

items.q: Which element is one of the halogens?
items.e: Iodine is in group 17.

items.q: Which element is one of the alkali metals?
items.e: Rubidium is in group 1.

items.q: What are the lanthanoids and actinoids?
items.e: Their last electron enters a 4f or 5f orbital.

items.q: Boron (B) and lithium (Li) are in the same period. Which has the larger atomic radius?
c: It cannot be predicted from the periodic table.
items.e: More protons pull the shells in across a period.

items.q: Which element has chemical properties most like bromine (Br)?
items.e: Same group = same number of valence electrons.

items.q: On what is the modern periodic law based?
items.e: Moseley showed the importance of atomic number.

items.q: Which group contains the noble gases?
items.e: They have full outer shells.

items.q: Which element is one of the alkali metals?
items.e: Sodium is in group 1.

items.q: In which group of the periodic table is Tc (Z = 43)?
items.e: Tc is in group 7 (the d-block).

items.q: Which element is one of the alkaline earth metals?
items.e: Magnesium is in group 2.

items.q: Which has the higher first ionization enthalpy, N or O?
items.e: N has a stable half-filled 2p³ configuration.

items.q: What is the oxide of sodium like?
items.e: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH.

items.q: Which family does fluorine (F) belong to?
items.e: Group 17 is the halogens.

items.q: Barium (Ba) and calcium (Ca) are in the same group. Which has the larger atomic radius?
c: It cannot be predicted from the periodic table.
items.e: More shells down a group.

items.q: What is the formula of the ion formed by aluminum?
items.e: Aluminum (Z = 13) loses 3 electrons.

items.q: Li<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 2 × (+1) + 1 × (−2) = 0.

items.q: What is the formula of calcium sulfide?
items.e: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is CaS.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the Li<sup>+</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 2 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What is the formula of calcium nitride?
items.e: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is Ca<sub>3</sub>N<sub>2</sub>.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the O<sup>2−</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 10 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What is the formula of potassium nitride?
items.e: K<sup>+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is K<sub>3</sub>N.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between hydrogen (H) and nitrogen (N)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: What is the formula of calcium oxide?
items.e: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is CaO.

items.q: K<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 2 × (+1) + 1 × (−2) = 0.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between lithium (Li) and phosphorus (P)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the S<sup>2−</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 18 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between magnesium (Mg) and zinc (Zn)?
items.e: Metal atoms share a sea of electrons.

items.q: What is the formula of potassium sulfide?
items.e: K<sup>+</sup> and S<sup>2−</sup>: the charges must balance, so the formula is K<sub>2</sub>S.

items.q: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and P<sup>3−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 3 × (+2) + 2 × (−3) = 0.

items.q: What is the electronic configuration of the Mg<sup>2+</sup> ion?
items.e: The ion has 10 electrons, the same arrangement as a noble gas.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between strontium (Sr) and iodine (I)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between magnesium (Mg) and oxygen (O)?
items.e: A metal gives electrons to a non-metal.

items.q: What kind of bond forms between hydrogen (H) and carbon (C)?
items.e: Two non-metals share electrons.

items.q: Ba<sup>2+</sup> and N<sup>3−</sup> ions combine. What is the formula of the compound?
items.e: Use the lowest numbers that make the total charge zero: 3 × (+2) + 2 × (−3) = 0.

items.q: Electronegativity: bromine (Br) = 2.96 and iodine (I) = 2.66. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 0.30. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: What is the shape of CCl<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom in CH<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: Carbon has 4 valence electrons; 4 are used in bonds, leaving 0 pairs.

items.q: Electronegativity: bromine (Br) = 2.96 and calcium (Ca) = 1.00. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 1.96. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: What is the shape of SF₆?
items.e: SF₆: octahedral.

items.q: Electronegativity: selenium (Se) = 2.55 and germanium (Ge) = 2.01. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 0.54. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: Oxygen (O) has 6 valence electrons. What is the formula of the simplest compound it forms with hydrogen?
items.e: It shares 2 electrons to fill its shell, so it bonds to 2 hydrogen atoms.

items.q: How many electrons are shared in a double covalent bond?
items.e: Each bond is one shared pair (2 electrons).

items.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom in PH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: Phosphorus has 5 valence electrons; 3 are used in bonds, leaving 1 pairs.

items.q: What is the shape of SiCl<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: 4 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs around the central atom: tetrahedral.

items.q: What is the shape of H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 1 lone pair around the central atom: pyramidal.

items.q: How many electrons are shared in a triple covalent bond?
items.e: Each bond is one shared pair (2 electrons).

items.q: What is the shape of H<sub>2</sub>S?
items.e: 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: bent (non-linear).

items.q: What is the hybridization of carbon in HCHO (the carbon)?
items.e: HCHO (the carbon): sp².

items.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom in SiH<sub>4</sub>?
items.e: Silicon has 4 valence electrons; 4 are used in bonds, leaving 0 pairs.

items.q: Electronegativity: hydrogen (H) = 2.20 and boron (B) = 2.04. What type of bond forms between them?
items.e: Difference = 0.16. Below 0.4: nonpolar; 0.4–1.7: polar covalent; above 1.7: ionic.

items.q: In a bond between rubidium (Rb) and fluorine (F) (electronegativities 0.82 and 3.98), which atom gets a partial negative charge?
c: Neither; the electrons are shared equally.
items.e: The more electronegative atom pulls the shared electrons closer.

items.q: What is the shape of BF₃?
items.e: BF₃: trigonal planar.

items.q: How many lone pairs are on the central atom in NH<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons; 3 are used in bonds, leaving 1 pairs.

items.q: What is the shape of ClF<sub>3</sub>?
items.e: 3 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around the central atom: T-shaped.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, hydrogen chloride (HCl) or magnesium oxide (MgO)?
c: It depends only on the container.
They boil at the same temperature.
items.e: Magnesium oxide has ionic attractions, which are stronger than the dipole-dipole forces in hydrogen chloride.

items.q: List from lowest to highest boiling point: butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>), octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>), pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>).
items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of ethanol (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: H bonded to N, O or F gives hydrogen bonding.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, fluorine (F<sub>2</sub>) or neon (Ne)?
c: It depends only on the container.
They boil at the same temperature.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; fluorine is larger (38 g/mol vs 20 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, butane (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) or nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>)?
c: It depends only on the container.
They boil at the same temperature.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; butane is larger (58 g/mol vs 28 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.

items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of magnesium oxide (MgO)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Ions attract each other strongly.

items.q: List from lowest to highest boiling point: hexane (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>), methane (CH<sub>4</sub>), octane (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>).
items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.

items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; octane is larger (114 g/mol vs 20 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of methanol (CH<sub>3</sub>OH)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: H bonded to N, O or F gives hydrogen bonding.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Nonpolar particles only have intermolecular forces.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of water (H<sub>2</sub>O)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: H bonded to N, O or F gives hydrogen bonding.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of acetone (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Polar molecules without H bonded to N, O or F have dipole-dipole forces.

items.q: List from lowest to highest boiling point: chlorine (Cl<sub>2</sub>), fluorine (F<sub>2</sub>), iodine (I<sub>2</sub>).
items.e: All have only intermolecular forces; more electrons (larger molar mass) means stronger forces.

items.q: What is the strongest attraction between particles of phosphine (PH<sub>3</sub>)?
c: ionic attractions (it is an ionic compound)
items.e: Polar molecules without H bonded to N, O or F have dipole-dipole forces.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, neon (Ne) or nitrogen (N<sub>2</sub>)?
c: It depends only on the container.
They boil at the same temperature.
items.e: Both have only intermolecular forces; nitrogen is larger (28 g/mol vs 20 g/mol), so its forces are stronger.

items.q: Which has the higher boiling point, hydrogen chloride (HCl) or hydrogen fluoride (HF)?
c: They boil at the same temperature.
It depends only on the container.
items.e: Hydrogen fluoride has hydrogen bonds, which are stronger than the dipole-dipole forces in hydrogen chloride.
